title: Frontal Recess Dissection (Draf I/IIa)
source_label: Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 9
indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyps involving the frontal sinus after failed appropriate medical therapy, recurrent acute frontal sinusitis, frontal mucoceles, and access for limited frontal pathology. Draf I clears obstructing cells below the frontal ostium; Draf IIa removes all recess cells between the lamina papyracea and middle turbinate and opens the ostium. Nearly all primary cases need no more than a IIa, done after maxillary antrostomy, sphenoidotomy, and complete ethmoidectomy.
setup: Head up 30 degrees (reverse Trendelenburg) with TIVA to reduce bleeding
Navigation registered with sagittal, coronal, and axial CT reconstructions loaded
30- and 70-degree endoscopes; frontal curettes, Bolger-Kuhn probes, giraffe through-cutting forceps, frontal Kerrison (Bachert) and mushroom punches
At least 2 mL local anesthetic with epinephrine at the superior middle turbinate attachment; 1:1000 epinephrine pledgets
landmarks: Agger nasi cell and its posterior wall
Anterior ethmoid artery in the skull base (posterior limit)
Suprabullar, frontal bullar, and supraorbital ethmoid cells
danger: Lateral lamella of the cribriform plate medially (drift with right hand)
Skull base just posterior to the recess
steps: Define the goal

Draf I clears cells below the frontal ostium; Draf IIa removes every recess cell between the lamina and the middle turbinate and opens the ostium. Plan for at most a IIa in nearly all primary cases, and perform it after antrostomy, sphenoidotomy, and complete ethmoidectomy have established the skull base and orbit.
Study the sagittal CT

Map the agger nasi, frontal cells (Kuhn types or IFAC agger, supra-agger, and supra-agger frontal cells), suprabullar, frontal bullar, supraorbital ethmoid, and intersinus septal cells. The anteroposterior diameter of the recess predicts difficulty; in very narrow recesses consider starting with balloon dilation.
Minimize bleeding

Raise the head about 30 degrees, use total intravenous anesthesia, inject at least 2 mL of local anesthetic with epinephrine at the superior middle turbinate attachment, and place 1:1000 epinephrine pledgets as needed. A dry field is essential for working with angled optics in a narrow space.
Use the right optics

Begin with a 30-degree scope, then switch to a 70-degree scope for the recess. Rotate the light post to lateralize the view, because a right-handed surgeon tends to drift medially toward the cribriform plate and lateral lamella.
Mark the posterior limit

Working from posterior to anterior along the skull base, identify the anterior ethmoid artery. It marks the posterior extent of the frontal dissection and the point beyond which instruments should not be pushed upward.
Find the transition zone

Look for the dark shadow of the drainage pathway, nearly always medial and posterior to the posterior wall of the agger nasi. Gently probe it with a curved suction or frontal curette and confirm with navigation before removing bone.
Remove the agger posterior wall

Take the posterior wall of the agger nasi with 45-degree front-to-back through-cutting giraffe forceps, or fracture it forward with a curette. This often exposes the frontal recess at once and shows the drainage pathway clearly.
Remove the medial wall

Cut the medial agger wall with front-to-back and side-to-side giraffe instruments, keeping in mind that the skull base lies posteriorly and the middle turbinate attachment medially. Use through-cutting instruments to preserve surrounding mucosa.
Remove the agger cap

Use a frontal Kerrison (Bachert) or 45-degree mushroom punch to take the cap from back to front up to the hard nasofrontal bone. This widens the recess more than any other single step and opens the frontal ostium.
Expand posteriorly

After re-identifying the anterior ethmoid artery, remove the ledge between any supraorbital ethmoid cell and the recess back to the skull base with a mushroom punch or giraffe forceps, so no partition remains to scar across the outflow.
Remove higher cells

Use Bolger-Kuhn probes and giraffe forceps to fracture and remove cells high in the recess or extending into the sinus, confirming position with navigation. Prefer through-cutters to avoid stripping mucosa, and use the debrider only to trim loose fragments.
Finish the opening

Trim some medial floor with a mushroom or Hosemann punch until the frontal sinus roof and posterior table are seen clearly with the 70-degree scope. Preserve mucosa circumferentially, since bare bone at the ostium promotes osteitis and stenosis.
Optional stent

In narrow or high-risk recesses place a rolled 0.25-0.5 mm silicone stent for 1-2 weeks or a steroid-eluting dissolvable implant for about 4 weeks, weighing cost and infection risk against fewer debridements and better patency.
exit_check: Frontal sinus roof and posterior table visible with 70-degree scope
No residual cell partitions or bone fragments in the recess
Mucosa preserved circumferentially; middle turbinate stable and medial
postop: Topical steroid irrigation as indicated for CRSwNP
Regular endoscopic debridement, keeping the middle turbinate medialized

early: CSF leak from lateral lamella or skull base injury
late: Persistent or recurrent frontal sinusitis needing Draf IIb/III

attending_followup: Differentiate Draf I, IIa, IIb, and III.

I: clears cells below the ostium; IIa: opens the ostium between lamina and middle turbinate; IIb: extends medially to the septum by removing the frontal floor; III: bilateral floors, upper septum, and intersinus septum removed.
What landmark marks the posterior limit of frontal recess dissection?
The anterior ethmoid artery in the skull base.
Where is the frontal drainage pathway relative to the agger nasi?
Usually medial and posterior to the posterior wall of the agger nasi cell.
Agger nasi, supra-agger, and supra-agger frontal cells.
Why does a right-handed surgeon need to rotate the 70-degree scope's light post?
To lateralize the view and avoid drifting medially into the cribriform plate and lateral lamella.
